Reference: Chen (2024)

Model Setting

The model studies the dynamic entry decisions of wind farm investors under uncertainty about the renewal of the Production Tax Credit (PTC). Time is discrete and indexed by year ttt. A wind farm iii first decides whether to enter the market or wait. Conditional on entry, it can either negotiate a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with a utility jjj, or sell to non-utility buyers such as corporations and merchant hedge counterparties.

The model therefore consists of three components: bilateral bargaining between wind farms and utilities, buyer choice and non-utility demand, and dynamic entry under policy uncertainty. The first two components determine the expected profit from entering in year ttt, while the dynamic problem determines the optimal timing of entry.

Bilateral Bargaining with Utilities

Suppose utility jjj signs a TTT-year PPA with wind farm iii in year ttt. The utility chooses wind capacity kijk_{ij}kij​ and pays a negotiated price pijp_{ij}pij​. Its discounted profit from the contract is:

πtU(pij,kij)=∑s=t+1t+TEtβs−t[(rs−pij)αikij+λs(αikij−Qjsgap)−hjs],(8.2.3.1)\pi_t^U(p_{ij},k_{ij}) = \sum_{s=t+1}^{t+T} E_t\beta^{s-t} \left[ (r_s-p_{ij})\alpha_i k_{ij} + \lambda_s(\alpha_i k_{ij}-Q^{gap}_{js}) - h_{js} \right], \tag{8.2.3.1}πtU​(pij​,kij​)=s=t+1∑t+T​Et​βs−t[(rs​−pij​)αi​kij​+λs​(αi​kij​−Qjsgap​)−hjs​],(8.2.3.1)

where rsr_srs​ is the electricity price, λs\lambda_sλs​ is the renewable credit price, αi\alpha_iαi​ is the productivity or capacity factor of wind farm iii, and QjsgapQ^{gap}_{js}Qjsgap​ measures utility jjj's unfulfilled renewable-energy demand under Renewable Portfolio Standards.

The hassle cost associated with the renewable credit market is:

hjs=δ(Qjsgap−αikij)Qjsgap.(8.2.3.2)h_{js} = \delta (Q^{gap}_{js}-\alpha_i k_{ij}) Q^{gap}_{js}. \tag{8.2.3.2}hjs​=δ(Qjsgap​−αi​kij​)Qjsgap​.(8.2.3.2)

A utility with a larger renewable portfolio gap therefore has a higher willingness to pay for additional wind capacity.

The wind farm receives revenues from the PPA and the PTC, and pays turbine costs:

πtW(pij,kij)=β(1−βT)1−βpijαikij+β(1−β10)1−βdtαikij−citkij,(8.2.3.3)\pi_t^W(p_{ij},k_{ij}) = \frac{\beta(1-\beta^T)}{1-\beta} p_{ij}\alpha_i k_{ij} + \frac{\beta(1-\beta^{10})}{1-\beta} d_t\alpha_i k_{ij} - c_{it}k_{ij}, \tag{8.2.3.3}πtW​(pij​,kij​)=1−ββ(1−βT)​pij​αi​kij​+1−ββ(1−β10)​dt​αi​kij​−cit​kij​,(8.2.3.3)

where dtd_tdt​ is the PTC subsidy and turbine costs are parameterized as:

cit=γ1Xit+kij2γ2.(8.2.3.4)c_{it} = \gamma_1X_{it} + \frac{k_{ij}}{2\gamma_2}. \tag{8.2.3.4}cit​=γ1​Xit​+2γ2​kij​​.(8.2.3.4)

The wind farm and the utility engage in Nash bargaining over both capacity and price:

max⁡kij,pij[πtU(pij,kij)−πtU(pij=∞)]ρ[πtW(pij,kij)−πtW(pij=∞)]1−ρ,(8.2.3.5)\max_{k_{ij},p_{ij}} \left[ \pi_t^U(p_{ij},k_{ij})-\pi_t^U(p_{ij}=\infty) \right]^\rho \left[ \pi_t^W(p_{ij},k_{ij})-\pi_t^W(p_{ij}=\infty) \right]^{1-\rho}, \tag{8.2.3.5}kij​,pij​max​[πtU​(pij​,kij​)−πtU​(pij​=∞)]ρ[πtW​(pij​,kij​)−πtW​(pij​=∞)]1−ρ,(8.2.3.5)

where ρ\rhoρ is the bargaining weight of the utility.

The optimal capacity equates utilities' marginal willingness to pay with the marginal turbine cost net of the PTC:

(∑s=t+1t+TEtβs−t[rs+λs(1−zs)+δQjsgap])αi=γ1Xit+kij∗γ2−β(1−β10)1−βdtαi+ξijt.(8.2.3.6)\left( \sum_{s=t+1}^{t+T} E_t\beta^{s-t} [r_s+\lambda_s(1-z_s)+\delta Q^{gap}_{js}] \right)\alpha_i = \gamma_1X_{it} + \frac{k_{ij}^*}{\gamma_2} - \frac{\beta(1-\beta^{10})}{1-\beta}d_t\alpha_i + \xi_{ijt}. \tag{8.2.3.6}(s=t+1∑t+T​Et​βs−t[rs​+λs​(1−zs​)+δQjsgap​])αi​=γ1​Xit​+γ2​kij∗​​−1−ββ(1−β10)​dt​αi​+ξijt​.(8.2.3.6)

The negotiated price divides the gains from trade between the two parties. A larger ρ\rhoρ implies that prices respond more strongly to turbine costs and less strongly to utilities' willingness to pay.

Non-Utility Demand and Buyer Choice

Wind farms can alternatively sell to non-utility buyers. Their demand for wind capacity is modeled using a linear demand function:

kinu=−ζ1pinu+ζ2αi+ζ3Xi+ζ4Zinu+υi,(8.2.3.7)k_i^{nu} = -\zeta_1p_i^{nu} + \zeta_2\alpha_i + \zeta_3X_i + \zeta_4Z_i^{nu} + \upsilon_i, \tag{8.2.3.7}kinu​=−ζ1​pinu​+ζ2​αi​+ζ3​Xi​+ζ4​Zinu​+υi​,(8.2.3.7)

where pinup_i^{nu}pinu​ is the wind energy price and ZinuZ_i^{nu}Zinu​ contains demand shifters.

A wind farm sells to a non-utility buyer with probability μm\mu_mμm​, which varies across markets. Conditional on selling to a utility, wind farm iii chooses among potential utilities j∈Jitj\in J_{it}j∈Jit​ according to:

max⁡j∈Jit{πtW(pij∗,kij∗)−γ31{mi≠mj}−γ4Distij+σϵij},(8.2.3.8)\max_{j\in J_{it}} \left\{ \pi_t^W(p_{ij}^*,k_{ij}^*) - \gamma_3\mathbb{1}\{m_i\neq m_j\} - \gamma_4Dist_{ij} + \sigma\epsilon_{ij} \right\}, \tag{8.2.3.8}j∈Jit​max​{πtW​(pij∗​,kij∗​)−γ3​1{mi​=mj​}−γ4​Distij​+σϵij​},(8.2.3.8)

where matching costs increase when the wind farm and utility are located in different states or farther apart. The shock ϵij\epsilon_{ij}ϵij​ follows the Type-I extreme value distribution.

The corresponding probability of matching with utility jjj is:

Pitbuyer(j)=(1−μm)exp⁡[πtW(pij∗,kij∗)−γ31{mi≠mj}−γ4Distijσ]∑l∈Jitexp⁡[πtW(pil∗,kil∗)−γ31{mi≠ml}−γ4Distilσ].(8.2.3.9)P_{it}^{buyer}(j) = (1-\mu_m) \frac{ \exp\left[ \frac{ \pi_t^W(p_{ij}^*,k_{ij}^*) -\gamma_3\mathbb{1}\{m_i\neq m_j\} -\gamma_4Dist_{ij} }{\sigma} \right] }{ \sum_{l\in J_{it}} \exp\left[ \frac{ \pi_t^W(p_{il}^*,k_{il}^*) -\gamma_3\mathbb{1}\{m_i\neq m_l\} -\gamma_4Dist_{il} }{\sigma} \right] }. \tag{8.2.3.9}Pitbuyer​(j)=(1−μm​)∑l∈Jit​​exp[σπtW​(pil∗​,kil∗​)−γ3​1{mi​=ml​}−γ4​Distil​​]exp[σπtW​(pij∗​,kij∗​)−γ3​1{mi​=mj​}−γ4​Distij​​]​.(8.2.3.9)

Integrating over buyer choices gives the ex-ante profit from entering:

πit=  μmπtnu+(1−μm)σ{log⁡[∑j∈Jitexp⁡(πtW(pij∗,kij∗)−γ31{mi≠mj}−γ4Distijσ)]+γE}.(8.2.3.10)\begin{aligned} \pi_{it} =&\; \mu_m\pi_t^{nu} +(1-\mu_m)\sigma \Bigg\{ \log\left[ \sum_{j\in J_{it}} \exp\left( \frac{ \pi_t^W(p_{ij}^*,k_{ij}^*) -\gamma_3\mathbb{1}\{m_i\neq m_j\} -\gamma_4Dist_{ij} }{\sigma} \right) \right] +\gamma_E \Bigg\}. \end{aligned} \tag{8.2.3.10}πit​=​μm​πtnu​+(1−μm​)σ{log​j∈Jit​∑​exp(σπtW​(pij∗​,kij∗​)−γ3​1{mi​=mj​}−γ4​Distij​​)​+γE​}.​(8.2.3.10)

Dynamic Entry under Policy Uncertainty

Projects that have remained in the interconnection queue for at least two years are treated as potential entrants. In year ttt, potential entrant iii faces an entry cost:

ψit=κWit+νit,(8.2.3.11)\psi_{it} = \kappa W_{it} + \nu_{it}, \tag{8.2.3.11}ψit​=κWit​+νit​,(8.2.3.11)

where WitW_{it}Wit​ is an observed entry-cost shifter, mainly state-level land prices, and the idiosyncratic cost shock follows an exponential distribution:

F(νit)=1−exp⁡(−νitϕ).(8.2.3.12)F(\nu_{it}) = 1-\exp\left(-\frac{\nu_{it}}{\phi}\right). \tag{8.2.3.12}F(νit​)=1−exp(−ϕνit​​).(8.2.3.12)

Let ωt∈{0,1}\omega_t\in\{0,1\}ωt​∈{0,1} denote the status of the PTC and sits_{it}sit​ denote the vector of other state variables. The value function is:

Vt(sit,ωt,νit)=max⁡{πit(sit,ωt)−κWit−νit,  βEt[Vt+1(sit+1,ωt+1,νit+1)∣sit,ωt]}.(8.2.3.13)V_t(s_{it},\omega_t,\nu_{it}) = \max \left\{ \pi_{it}(s_{it},\omega_t) - \kappa W_{it} - \nu_{it}, \; \beta E_t [ V_{t+1}(s_{it+1},\omega_{t+1},\nu_{it+1}) \mid s_{it},\omega_t ] \right\}. \tag{8.2.3.13}Vt​(sit​,ωt​,νit​)=max{πit​(sit​,ωt​)−κWit​−νit​,βEt​[Vt+1​(sit+1​,ωt+1​,νit+1​)∣sit​,ωt​]}.(8.2.3.13)

The investor enters when current net profits exceed the option value of waiting. Because νit\nu_{it}νit​ follows an exponential distribution, the entry probability has the closed form:

PtE(sit,ωt)=1−exp⁡[−πit−κWit−βEt[Vt+1]ϕ].(8.2.3.14)P_t^E(s_{it},\omega_t) = 1- \exp \left[ - \frac{ \pi_{it} - \kappa W_{it} - \beta E_t[V_{t+1}] }{\phi} \right]. \tag{8.2.3.14}PtE​(sit​,ωt​)=1−exp[−ϕπit​−κWit​−βEt​[Vt+1​]​].(8.2.3.14)

The crucial determinant of the continuation value is the investor's belief about future PTC renewal. Let

bt=Pr⁡(ωt+1=1∣ωt=1)(8.2.3.15)b_t = \Pr(\omega_{t+1}=1\mid\omega_t=1) \tag{8.2.3.15}bt​=Pr(ωt+1​=1∣ωt​=1)(8.2.3.15)

denote the perceived probability that the PTC is renewed for another year. A lower btb_tbt​ reduces the expected value of waiting and therefore increases current entry.

Policy Beliefs

Since an unrestricted sequence of future beliefs cannot be identified from observed entry decisions, the model imposes two restrictions.

First, policy termination is an absorbing state:

Pr⁡(ωt+1=0∣ωt=0)=1.(8.2.3.16)\Pr(\omega_{t+1}=0\mid\omega_t=0)=1. \tag{8.2.3.16}Pr(ωt+1​=0∣ωt​=0)=1.(8.2.3.16)

Thus, if the PTC expires, investors believe that it will never return. The value function without the PTC is stationary:

V0(sit,νit)=max⁡{π0(sit)−κWit−νit,  βE[V0(sit+1,νit+1)∣sit]}.(8.2.3.17)V^0(s_{it},\nu_{it}) = \max \left\{ \pi^0(s_{it}) - \kappa W_{it} - \nu_{it}, \; \beta E[V^0(s_{it+1},\nu_{it+1})\mid s_{it}] \right\}. \tag{8.2.3.17}V0(sit​,νit​)=max{π0(sit​)−κWit​−νit​,βE[V0(sit+1​,νit+1​)∣sit​]}.(8.2.3.17)

Second, conditional on the policy remaining active, investors in year ttt apply the same perceived one-year renewal probability btb_tbt​ to all future years. Beliefs can nevertheless change across cohorts as new information arrives. The value function when the PTC is currently active becomes:

V1(sit,νit;bt)=max⁡{π1(sit)−κWit−νit,β[btE[V1(sit+1,νit+1;bt)∣sit]+(1−bt)E[V0(sit+1,νit+1)∣sit]]}.(8.2.3.18)\begin{aligned} V^1(s_{it},\nu_{it};b_t) = \max \Big\{ & \pi^1(s_{it}) - \kappa W_{it} - \nu_{it}, \\ & \beta \left[ b_tE[V^1(s_{it+1},\nu_{it+1};b_t)\mid s_{it}] +(1-b_t) E[V^0(s_{it+1},\nu_{it+1})\mid s_{it}] \right] \Big\}. \end{aligned} \tag{8.2.3.18}V1(sit​,νit​;bt​)=max{​π1(sit​)−κWit​−νit​,β[bt​E[V1(sit+1​,νit+1​;bt​)∣sit​]+(1−bt​)E[V0(sit+1​,νit+1​)∣sit​]]}.​(8.2.3.18)

These assumptions transform the original non-stationary problem into a sequence of cohort-specific stationary dynamic problems indexed by btb_tbt​.

State Variables and Equilibrium

The state vector contains three groups of variables. The first group consists of time-varying exogenous states, including average turbine productivity, turbine prices, subsidy levels, electricity prices, and renewable credit prices. Their transitions are modeled as AR(1) processes.

The second group contains time-invariant project characteristics that affect utility demand, non-utility demand, and matching costs.

The third group captures the endogenous evolution of utilities' renewable demand. Since tracking the renewable portfolio gap of every potential utility is computationally infeasible, the model summarizes buyer-side demand using the inclusive value:

Φit=πit({Qjtgap}j∈Jit)−πit({Qjtgap=0}j∈Jit).(8.2.3.19)\Phi_{it} = \pi_{it}(\{Q^{gap}_{jt}\}_{j\in J_{it}}) - \pi_{it}(\{Q^{gap}_{jt}=0\}_{j\in J_{it}}). \tag{8.2.3.19}Φit​=πit​({Qjtgap​}j∈Jit​​)−πit​({Qjtgap​=0}j∈Jit​​).(8.2.3.19)

More wind capacity entering today reduces utilities' future renewable portfolio gaps and therefore lowers future Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​. Its transition depends on lagged new wind capacity KmtK_{mt}Kmt​. The model uses a moment-based Markov equilibrium in which investors form expectations about these aggregate industry states and make entry decisions according to their perceived policy beliefs.

Identification and Estimation: Bargaining and Buyer Choice

The optimal capacity and pricing equations are jointly estimated by nonlinear least squares. The turbine-cost convexity parameter γ2\gamma_2γ2​ is identified by how negotiated capacity responds to the per-unit subsidy. The hassle-cost parameter δ\deltaδ is identified by the effect of utilities' renewable portfolio gaps on negotiated capacity.

The bargaining parameter ρ\rhoρ is identified from the relative pass-through of utilities' willingness to pay and turbine costs into negotiated PPA prices. A larger ρ\rhoρ implies that negotiated prices move more closely with wind farm costs and less closely with utility willingness to pay.

The non-utility demand equation is estimated using instrumental variables because pinup_i^{nu}pinu​ is correlated with unobserved demand shocks. The instruments include renewable credit prices, agricultural land prices, and state-level wind energy tax and recruitment policies.

The buyer choice model is estimated by maximum likelihood. Matching-cost parameters (γ3,γ4)(\gamma_3,\gamma_4)(γ3​,γ4​) are identified by how matching probabilities vary with state borders and geographic distance, while σ\sigmaσ is identified by residual variation in utility choices. The non-utility probabilities μm\mu_mμm​ are identified by observed frequencies of non-utility contracts across markets.

Identification and Estimation: Dynamic Entry

The main identification challenge is to separate the entry-cost parameters (κ,ϕ)(\kappa,\phi)(κ,ϕ) from the policy-belief parameters btb_tbt​. High observed entry can result either from low entry costs or from pessimistic beliefs about future PTC renewal.

The identification strategy exploits variation in the policy regime over time. The baseline estimation assumes no policy uncertainty during 2014–2018:

bt=1.(8.2.3.20)b_t=1. \tag{8.2.3.20}bt​=1.(8.2.3.20)

The relatively stable entry behavior in this period is used to identify the entry-cost distribution. The model uses 2013–2018 as an alternative specification.

For the stable-policy period, the dynamic problem is stationary:

V(sit,νit)=max⁡{π(sit)−κWit−νit,  β∫V(sit+1,νit+1)dG(sit+1∣sit)dF(νit+1)}.(8.2.3.21)V(s_{it},\nu_{it}) = \max \left\{ \pi(s_{it}) - \kappa W_{it} - \nu_{it}, \; \beta \int V(s_{it+1},\nu_{it+1}) dG(s_{it+1}\mid s_{it}) dF(\nu_{it+1}) \right\}. \tag{8.2.3.21}V(sit​,νit​)=max{π(sit​)−κWit​−νit​,β∫V(sit+1​,νit+1​)dG(sit+1​∣sit​)dF(νit+1​)}.(8.2.3.21)

The profit and value functions are approximated using quadratic basis functions of the state variables:

V(sit)≈∑l=1LγlVul(sit).(8.2.3.22)V(s_{it}) \approx \sum_{l=1}^{L} \gamma_l^V u_l(s_{it}). \tag{8.2.3.22}V(sit​)≈l=1∑L​γlV​ul​(sit​).(8.2.3.22)

The entry-cost parameters are estimated by matching model-predicted state-year entry rates with observed entry rates:

(κ^,ϕ^)=arg⁡min⁡κ,ϕ∑m,t(P^mtE−PmtE)2,(8.2.3.23)(\hat{\kappa},\hat{\phi}) = \arg\min_{\kappa,\phi} \sum_{m,t} \left( \widehat{P}_{mt}^E - P_{mt}^E \right)^2, \tag{8.2.3.23}(κ^,ϕ^​)=argκ,ϕmin​m,t∑​(PmtE​−PmtE​)2,(8.2.3.23)

where the predicted state-level entry rate averages individual predicted probabilities across potential entrants.

Conditional on (κ^,ϕ^)(\hat{\kappa},\hat{\phi})(κ^,ϕ^​), policy beliefs are identified from investment bunching in earlier policy-expiration years. For each candidate btb_tbt​, the model solves V0V^0V0 and V1V^1V1, allowing the equilibrium transition of endogenous states such as KmtK_{mt}Kmt​ and Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ to adjust with the implied entry behavior. The individual predicted entry probability is:

P^tE(sit;bt)=1−exp⁡[−π^(sit)−κ^Wit−β[btV^1(sit;bt)+(1−bt)V^0(sit;bt)]ϕ^].(8.2.3.24)\widehat{P}_t^E(s_{it};b_t) = 1- \exp \left[ - \frac{ \widehat{\pi}(s_{it}) - \hat{\kappa}W_{it} - \beta \left[ b_t\widehat{V}^1(s_{it};b_t) + (1-b_t)\widehat{V}^0(s_{it};b_t) \right] }{\hat{\phi}} \right]. \tag{8.2.3.24}PtE​(sit​;bt​)=1−exp​−ϕ^​π(sit​)−κ^Wit​−β[bt​V1(sit​;bt​)+(1−bt​)V0(sit​;bt​)]​​.(8.2.3.24)

The belief parameter is estimated separately for each year by matching predicted and observed state-level entry rates:

b^t=arg⁡min⁡bt∑m(P^mtE(bt)−PmtE)2.(8.2.3.25)\hat{b}_t = \arg\min_{b_t} \sum_m \left( \widehat{P}_{mt}^E(b_t) - P_{mt}^E \right)^2. \tag{8.2.3.25}b^t​=argbt​min​m∑​(PmtE​(bt​)−PmtE​)2.(8.2.3.25)

Thus, later stable-policy years identify the entry-cost distribution, while excess entry and bunching around earlier expiration dates identify investors' perceived probability of policy renewal.

Key Estimates

The estimated bargaining weight of utilities is approximately 0.670.670.67, implying that utilities capture about two thirds of the gains from trade. The estimated price elasticity of non-utility wind demand is approximately −1.6-1.6−1.6, and about 24%24\%24% of wind farms sell to non-utility buyers.

The estimated mean realized entry cost conditional on entry is approximately $35 million. Most importantly, the perceived PTC renewal probability for the 2011 cohort is only around 0.30.30.3, while it recovers to approximately 0.840.840.84 for the 2012 cohort. The low estimated belief in 2011 generates a low continuation value of waiting and accounts for the large investment spike around the policy expiration date.

This is the utility's objective: the expected present value, over the TTT contract years s=t+1,…,t+Ts=t+1,\dots,t+Ts=t+1,…,t+T, of what the contract with wind farm iii is worth to utility jjj. Each year the wind farm delivers αikij\alpha_i k_{ij}αi​kij​ units of energy (capacity kijk_{ij}kij​ times capacity factor αi\alpha_iαi​). The bracket has three parts. The first, (rs−pij)αikij(r_s-p_{ij})\alpha_i k_{ij}(rs​−pij​)αi​kij​, is the energy margin: the utility resells at the electricity price rsr_srs​ what it buys at the fixed contract price pijp_{ij}pij​. The second, λs(αikij−Qjsgap)\lambda_s(\alpha_i k_{ij}-Q^{gap}_{js})λs​(αi​kij​−Qjsgap​), is the net position in the renewable credit market: wind output generates credits worth λs\lambda_sλs​ each, while the gap QjsgapQ^{gap}_{js}Qjsgap​ must be covered; when output is below the gap the term is negative and equals the cost of buying the missing credits. The third, hjsh_{js}hjs​, is the non-pecuniary hassle cost of relying on the credit market, defined in equation (2). Payments start one year after signing, so the first flow is discounted by β\betaβ, and EtE_tEt​ averages over future rsr_srs​, λs\lambda_sλs​ and QjsgapQ^{gap}_{js}Qjsgap​ given year-ttt information.

Substituting equation (2) makes the role of capacity transparent, because the per-year payoff is linear in αikij\alpha_i k_{ij}αi​kij​:

(rs−pij)αikij+λs(αikij−Qjsgap)−hjs=(rs−pij+λs+δQjsgap)αikij−λsQjsgap−δ(Qjsgap)2.(r_s-p_{ij})\alpha_i k_{ij}+\lambda_s(\alpha_i k_{ij}-Q^{gap}_{js})-h_{js} =\left(r_s-p_{ij}+\lambda_s+\delta Q^{gap}_{js}\right)\alpha_i k_{ij}-\lambda_s Q^{gap}_{js}-\delta\left(Q^{gap}_{js}\right)^2 .(rs​−pij​)αi​kij​+λs​(αi​kij​−Qjsgap​)−hjs​=(rs​−pij​+λs​+δQjsgap​)αi​kij​−λs​Qjsgap​−δ(Qjsgap​)2.

The coefficient rs+λs+δQjsgapr_s+\lambda_s+\delta Q^{gap}_{js}rs​+λs​+δQjsgap​ is the utility's willingness to pay per unit of wind energy; the last two terms do not depend on the contract and are what the utility gets with no contract. This expression is the building block of the Nash product in equation (5) and of the left-hand side of the capacity condition (6). The formulation rules out risk aversion and any curvature of utility profit in kijk_{ij}kij​; all curvature in the bargaining problem comes from turbine costs in equation (4).

The hassle cost is an assumed functional form. The factor Qjsgap−αikijQ^{gap}_{js}-\alpha_i k_{ij}Qjsgap​−αi​kij​ is the part of the renewable portfolio gap that is still uncovered after the contract, that is, the volume of credits utility jjj must procure on the credit market in year sss. This shortfall is multiplied by the gap itself and by δ>0\delta>0δ>0, so that the cost per uncovered unit, δQjsgap\delta Q^{gap}_{js}δQjsgap​, is larger for utilities that are further from compliance. The cost is in money units per year and is separate from the market price of credits λs\lambda_sλs​ that already appears in equation (1); it stands for transaction costs, search, regulatory risk and the like.

Two derivatives summarize what the form buys:

−∂hjs∂(αikij)=δQjsgap,hjs∣kij=0=δ(Qjsgap)2.-\frac{\partial h_{js}}{\partial(\alpha_i k_{ij})}=\delta Q^{gap}_{js}, \qquad h_{js}\big|_{k_{ij}=0}=\delta\left(Q^{gap}_{js}\right)^2 .−∂(αi​kij​)∂hjs​​=δQjsgap​,hjs​​kij​=0​=δ(Qjsgap​)2.

The marginal benefit of one more unit of wind energy is constant in kijk_{ij}kij​ and proportional to the gap, and the total hassle without any contract is quadratic in the gap. This is exactly the term δQjsgap\delta Q^{gap}_{js}δQjsgap​ in the willingness to pay of equation (6): a utility with a larger gap bargains for more capacity, and this cross-utility and over-time variation in gaps identifies δ\deltaδ. With δ=0\delta=0δ=0 the gap would only enter utility profit as a constant and would not affect the contract at all. The form is meant for αikij≤Qjsgap\alpha_i k_{ij}\le Q^{gap}_{js}αi​kij​≤Qjsgap​; if contracted output exceeded the gap the formula would turn into a benefit, which the note does not discuss.

Two things are worth noticing. The PPA payment that the wind farm receives is exactly the payment that the utility makes in equation (1), so pijp_{ij}pij​ is a pure transfer between the two parties; this is what makes the bargaining solution in equation (6) so simple. The parties choose capacity and price jointly. Because the price is a pure transfer, the solution has a two-step structure derived under equation (6): kijk_{ij}kij​ is chosen to maximize the joint surplus, and pijp_{ij}pij​ splits that surplus in proportions ρ\rhoρ and 1−ρ1-\rho1−ρ. The formulation treats each pair in isolation: the disagreement point does not include the option of contracting with another partner. This is the demand for wind capacity by non-utility buyers (corporations and merchant hedge counterparties), assumed linear rather than derived from a bargaining problem. The dependent variable kinuk_i^{nu}kinu​ is the capacity that such buyers take from wind farm iii. It decreases in the wind energy price pinup_i^{nu}pinu​ with slope ζ1>0\zeta_1>0ζ1​>0, increases with the farm's productivity αi\alpha_iαi​ if ζ2>0\zeta_2>0ζ2​>0, and shifts with project characteristics XiX_iXi​ and with demand shifters ZinuZ_i^{nu}Zinu​ that are specific to the non-utility segment. The error υi\upsilon_iυi​ collects unobserved demand shocks. The equation plays for the non-utility channel the role that equation (6) plays for utilities: together with the cost side in equations (3) and (4) it delivers the profit πtnu\pi_t^{nu}πtnu​ from selling to a non-utility buyer, which enters the ex-ante profit in equation (10).

Linearity implies a price elasticity that varies along the curve:

∂kinu∂pinupinukinu=−ζ1pinukinu,\frac{\partial k_i^{nu}}{\partial p_i^{nu}}\frac{p_i^{nu}}{k_i^{nu}}=-\zeta_1\frac{p_i^{nu}}{k_i^{nu}},∂pinu​∂kinu​​kinu​pinu​​=−ζ1​kinu​pinu​​,

and the value of about −1.6-1.6−1.6 reported in the note is this expression evaluated at the estimates and typical values of price and capacity. Ordinary least squares would be biased because a buyer with a high υi\upsilon_iυi​ pays a higher price, so pinup_i^{nu}pinu​ is correlated with the error and the slope would be attenuated toward zero or even of the wrong sign. The equation is therefore estimated by instrumental variables, using supply-side shifters excluded from non-utility demand: renewable credit prices, agricultural land prices and state wind tax and recruitment policies. Identification of ζ1\zeta_1ζ1​ comes from price variation induced by these instruments.

This is the wind farm's discrete choice of a utility partner, conditional on selling to a utility. For each candidate jjj in the choice set JitJ_{it}Jit​, the farm anticipates the outcome of bargaining, so the first term is its profit πtW(pij∗,kij∗)\pi_t^W(p_{ij}^*,k_{ij}^*)πtW​(pij∗​,kij∗​) at the negotiated price and capacity from equation (6). From it the farm subtracts matching costs: a fixed penalty γ3\gamma_3γ3​ if the utility is in a different state, mi≠mjm_i\neq m_jmi​=mj​ (regulatory and transmission barriers across state borders), and a cost γ4\gamma_4γ4​ per unit of distance DistijDist_{ij}Distij​. The last term is an idiosyncratic match shock ϵij\epsilon_{ij}ϵij​, distributed Type-I extreme value and independent across utilities, scaled by σ\sigmaσ.

All terms are in money units because profit enters with a coefficient of one. This is why the scale σ\sigmaσ is identified rather than normalized: dividing the objective by σ\sigmaσ gives a standard logit in which the coefficient on profit is 1/σ1/\sigma1/σ, so σ\sigmaσ is recovered from how strongly choices respond to differences in profit across utilities, and γ3\gamma_3γ3​, γ4\gamma_4γ4​ are expressed in dollars. A small σ\sigmaσ means that farms almost always pick the most profitable utility; a large σ\sigmaσ means that matches are close to random. The extreme value assumption delivers the closed-form choice probability in equation (9) and the closed-form expected maximum in equation (10), at the price of the independence of irrelevant alternatives property: the relative odds of two utilities do not depend on which other utilities are available. The choice is one-sided, so a utility is assumed to accept any farm that selects it.

Let vijv_{ij}vij​ denote the deterministic part of the objective in equation (8),

The log-sum term rises with the number of nearby utilities and with their willingness to pay, so πit\pi_{it}πit​ summarizes the whole buyer side in a single number; this is what the dynamic model in equation (13) takes as the payoff from entry. This specifies the sunk cost that potential entrant iii must pay if it enters in year ttt. It is the sum of a systematic component κWit\kappa W_{it}κWit​ and an idiosyncratic shock νit\nu_{it}νit​. The shifter WitW_{it}Wit​ is observed by the econometrician and is mainly the state-level price of land, so κ\kappaκ converts land prices into entry costs and is expected to be positive. The shock νit\nu_{it}νit​ is private information of the investor, drawn afresh every year and independently across projects from the distribution in equation (12); it captures permitting delays, local opposition, interconnection upgrade costs and other project-specific frictions. Both components are in the same money units as the profit πit\pi_{it}πit​ of equation (10).

The entry cost is distinct from the turbine cost of equation (4): the turbine cost depends on capacity and is already netted out of πit\pi_{it}πit​, while ψit\psi_{it}ψit​ is a fixed cost of entering at all. It is what makes timing a real decision. A project with a bad draw of νit\nu_{it}νit​ this year may prefer to wait for a better draw, as long as the profit from entering later is not much lower; this is the option value in equation (13). Because investors enter only when νit\nu_{it}νit​ is low enough, the costs actually paid are selected from the lower tail, which is why the note reports the mean realized entry cost conditional on entry (about 35 million dollars) rather than the unconditional mean κWit+ϕ\kappa W_{it}+\phiκWit​+ϕ. The additive form means WitW_{it}Wit​ shifts the entry threshold one for one, which is how κ\kappaκ is identified from the covariation of entry rates with land prices in equation (23).

The idiosyncratic entry-cost shock is assumed exponential with scale parameter ϕ>0\phi>0ϕ>0. The shock is non-negative, its density is f(ν)=1ϕexp⁡(−ν/ϕ)f(\nu)=\frac{1}{\phi}\exp(-\nu/\phi)f(ν)=ϕ1​exp(−ν/ϕ), and its mean and standard deviation both equal ϕ\phiϕ, so a single parameter governs both the level and the dispersion of entry costs. Together with κ\kappaκ of equation (11), ϕ\phiϕ is one of the two entry-cost parameters estimated in equation (23).

The assumption buys closed forms. An investor enters when νit\nu_{it}νit​ falls below a threshold xxx (the net gain from entering now instead of waiting), so the entry probability is F(x)=1−exp⁡(−x/ϕ)F(x)=1-\exp(-x/\phi)F(x)=1−exp(−x/ϕ), which is equation (14). Two further integrals used later are

∫0x(x−ν)1ϕe−ν/ϕdν=x−ϕF(x),E[ν∣ν≤x]=ϕ−x e−x/ϕF(x).\int_0^{x}(x-\nu)\frac{1}{\phi}e^{-\nu/\phi}d\nu=x-\phi F(x), \qquad E[\nu\mid\nu\le x]=\phi-\frac{x\,e^{-x/\phi}}{F(x)} .∫0x​(x−ν)ϕ1​e−ν/ϕdν=x−ϕF(x),E[ν∣ν≤x]=ϕ−F(x)xe−x/ϕ​.

The first gives the expected value of the option to enter and hence the integrated Bellman equation under equation (21); the second gives the mean realized shock conditional on entry. The parameter ϕ\phiϕ also controls how sensitive entry is to incentives: the derivative of the entry probability with respect to the threshold is (1−F(x))/ϕ(1-F(x))/\phi(1−F(x))/ϕ. A small ϕ\phiϕ makes entry respond sharply to changes in profit or in the continuation value, so the same bunching before a policy deadline would be rationalized with a smaller change in beliefs; this is why ϕ\phiϕ must be pinned down from a period without policy uncertainty before beliefs can be estimated. Because the support is [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), the formula implies zero entry whenever the threshold is negative.

This is the Bellman equation of a potential entrant, an optimal stopping problem. The state consists of the vector sits_{it}sit​ (prices, productivity, subsidy level, project characteristics and the inclusive value of equation (19)), the policy status ωt∈{0,1}\omega_t\in\{0,1\}ωt​∈{0,1}, with ωt=1\omega_t=1ωt​=1 when the PTC is in force, and the private cost shock νit\nu_{it}νit​. The investor compares two options. Entering now yields the ex-ante profit πit(sit,ωt)\pi_{it}(s_{it},\omega_t)πit​(sit​,ωt​) of equation (10), which depends on ωt\omega_tωt​ because the subsidy dtd_tdt​ enters the wind farm's profit in equation (3), minus the entry cost κWit+νit\kappa W_{it}+\nu_{it}κWit​+νit​ of equation (11). Waiting yields no flow payoff today and the discounted expected value of facing the same choice next year with a new state, a possibly different policy status and a new cost draw.

Entry is a terminal action: the entire value of an operating wind farm is contained in πit\pi_{it}πit​, already a present value over the contract, so there is no continuation value after entry. The time subscript on VtV_tVt​ signals that the problem is in general non-stationary, since beliefs about future policy may differ from year to year. The expectation EtE_tEt​ is taken over three things: the transition of sits_{it}sit​, the policy transition governed by the belief in equation (15), and the next draw νit+1\nu_{it+1}νit+1​. The key economic force is the option value of waiting. If the investor believes the PTC will lapse, the continuation value with ωt+1=0\omega_{t+1}=0ωt+1​=0 is low, the second argument of the max falls, and entry today becomes more attractive; this generates investment bunching before expiration dates. The decision rule is a cutoff in νit\nu_{it}νit​, derived in equation (14). The restrictions in equations (16) to (18) make the problem tractable.

Start from the Bellman equation (13). The investor enters in year ttt if and only if the first argument of the max is at least as large as the second:

πit−κWit−νit ≥ βEt[Vt+1].\pi_{it}-\kappa W_{it}-\nu_{it}\ \ge\ \beta E_t[V_{t+1}].πit​−κWit​−νit​ ≥ βEt​[Vt+1​].

The continuation value on the right does not depend on the current shock νit\nu_{it}νit​, because shocks are independent over time and νit\nu_{it}νit​ does not affect the transition of the other states. The condition is therefore a cutoff rule in the shock,

νit ≤ νˉit≡πit−κWit−βEt[Vt+1],\nu_{it}\ \le\ \bar\nu_{it}\equiv\pi_{it}-\kappa W_{it}-\beta E_t[V_{t+1}],νit​ ≤ νˉit​≡πit​−κWit​−βEt​[Vt+1​],

where νˉit\bar\nu_{it}νˉit​ is the net gain from entering now rather than waiting, before the idiosyncratic cost. The entry probability conditional on the states observed by the econometrician is the probability of this event. Using the exponential CDF in equation (12),

PtE(sit,ωt)=Pr⁡(νit≤νˉit)=F(νˉit)=1−exp⁡[−πit−κWit−βEt[Vt+1]ϕ].P_t^E(s_{it},\omega_t)=\Pr\left(\nu_{it}\le\bar\nu_{it}\right)=F(\bar\nu_{it}) =1-\exp\left[-\frac{\pi_{it}-\kappa W_{it}-\beta E_t[V_{t+1}]}{\phi}\right].PtE​(sit​,ωt​)=Pr(νit​≤νˉit​)=F(νˉit​)=1−exp[−ϕπit​−κWit​−βEt​[Vt+1​]​].

If νˉit<0\bar\nu_{it}<0νˉit​<0 no draw of the shock justifies entry and the probability is zero, so in general

PtE(sit,ωt)=1−exp⁡[−max⁡{νˉit,0}ϕ].P_t^E(s_{it},\omega_t)=1-\exp\left[-\frac{\max\{\bar\nu_{it},0\}}{\phi}\right].PtE​(sit​,ωt​)=1−exp[−ϕmax{νˉit​,0}​].

The comparative statics are immediate. The probability increases in current profit πit\pi_{it}πit​, decreases in the cost shifter WitW_{it}Wit​ when κ>0\kappa>0κ>0, and decreases in the continuation value βEt[Vt+1]\beta E_t[V_{t+1}]βEt​[Vt+1​]. Anything that lowers the value of waiting, such as a lower perceived probability that the PTC survives, raises entry today. Inverting the formula gives νˉit=−ϕlog⁡(1−PtE)\bar\nu_{it}=-\phi\log(1-P_t^E)νˉit​=−ϕlog(1−PtE​), which shows how observed entry rates reveal the net gain from entering once ϕ\phiϕ is known.

This defines the belief parameter that the paper sets out to measure. btb_tbt​ is the probability that investors in year ttt assign to the PTC still being in force next year, given that it is in force now. It is a perceived (subjective) probability: nothing requires it to coincide with the objective frequency of renewal, and in fact the PTC was always eventually renewed in the sample. The subscript ttt allows beliefs to change from one year to the next as news arrives.

The belief enters the model only through the continuation value in equation (13). Splitting the expectation over tomorrow's policy status,

Et[Vt+1]=bt Et[Vt+1∣ωt+1=1]+(1−bt) Et[Vt+1∣ωt+1=0],E_t[V_{t+1}]=b_t\,E_t[V_{t+1}\mid\omega_{t+1}=1]+(1-b_t)\,E_t[V_{t+1}\mid\omega_{t+1}=0],Et​[Vt+1​]=bt​Et​[Vt+1​∣ωt+1​=1]+(1−bt​)Et​[Vt+1​∣ωt+1​=0],

and since the value with the subsidy exceeds the value without it, the continuation value is increasing in btb_tbt​. By equation (14) a lower btb_tbt​ therefore raises current entry: pessimistic investors rush to enter while the subsidy is still available.

A full belief system would specify the perceived renewal probability at every future date, which entry data cannot identify. Combined with the absorbing-state assumption in equation (16) and the constant-belief assumption behind equation (18), a single number per cohort is enough. Under those assumptions the perceived probability that the policy survives nnn more years is btnb_t^nbtn​, and the expected number of further years with the subsidy is

∑n=1∞bt n=bt1−bt.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_t^{\,n}=\frac{b_t}{1-b_t}.n=1∑∞​btn​=1−bt​bt​​.

At the estimates in the note this is about 0.430.430.43 years for the 2011 cohort (bt≈0.3b_t\approx0.3bt​≈0.3) and about 5.255.255.25 years for the 2012 cohort (bt≈0.84b_t\approx0.84bt​≈0.84).

This is the first identifying restriction on beliefs: expiration of the PTC is an absorbing state. Once the policy is off, ωt=0\omega_t=0ωt​=0, investors assign probability one to it staying off forever, and so probability zero to reinstatement. Together with equation (15), the perceived policy process is a two-state Markov chain with transition matrix (rows are today's status 111 and 000, columns tomorrow's status 111 and 000)

(bt1−bt01).\begin{pmatrix} b_t & 1-b_t\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}.(bt​0​1−bt​1​).

The restriction does two jobs. First, it removes a second belief parameter, the probability of reinstatement after a lapse, which could not be separated from btb_tbt​ using entry data: a high entry rate before a deadline could reflect either a low chance of renewal or a low chance of later reinstatement. Second, it makes the no-subsidy world stationary, which yields the simple Bellman equation (17) for V0V^0V0; this value is the outside option that appears in the continuation value of equation (18).

The assumption is strong relative to history, since the PTC did lapse and was reinstated (sometimes retroactively) several times. It should be read as a normalization of what btb_tbt​ means: the estimated btb_tbt​ is the perceived probability that the subsidy remains available in the sense relevant for the investor's decision, with any perceived chance of reinstatement folded into it. If investors in fact expected a lapsed subsidy to return with positive probability, waiting would be more valuable than the model assumes, and rationalizing the same bunching would require an even lower probability of on-time renewal than the estimated btb_tbt​. The direction of the main finding, low perceived renewal probability in years with strong bunching, does not depend on this.

The continuation value is an expectation over tomorrow's policy status, state and shock. The model therefore solves one stationary problem per cohort: investors of year ttt behave as if btb_tbt​ were permanent, and investors of year t+1t+1t+1 re-solve with bt+1b_{t+1}bt+1​. This is a form of anticipated-utility behavior, since investors do not anticipate that their own beliefs will be revised. Two limiting cases are useful. This defines the state variable that summarizes the buyer side of the market for project iii. The ex-ante profit πit\pi_{it}πit​ of equation (10) depends on the renewable portfolio gaps of all utilities in the choice set JitJ_{it}Jit​, because each gap raises that utility's willingness to pay through the term δQjsgap\delta Q^{gap}_{js}δQjsgap​ in equation (6). Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ is the difference between the ex-ante profit at the actual gaps and the ex-ante profit that would obtain if every utility's gap were zero. It is thus the part of expected entry profit, in money units, that is due to unfulfilled RPS demand; it is non-negative when δ>0\delta>0δ>0 and equals zero when no nearby utility has a gap.

The purpose is dimension reduction. The exact state would include the gap of every potential utility partner, and each gap evolves endogenously as utilities sign contracts, which is computationally infeasible. Because gaps matter to an entrant only through πit\pi_{it}πit​, the scalar Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ is treated as a sufficient summary, and investors are assumed to forecast it with a low-dimensional Markov process rather than tracking each gap. The term inclusive value refers to the log-sum form of πit\pi_{it}πit​: Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ is a difference of two log-sums over utilities.

The variable is what makes entry decisions interact. Capacity that enters today fills utilities' gaps, so higher lagged new capacity KmtK_{mt}Kmt​ in the market lowers future Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ and hence the future profit of waiting projects. This competition for scarce utility demand is an additional reason to enter early. In the moment-based Markov equilibrium, the perceived transition of Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ as a function of KmtK_{mt}Kmt​ must be consistent with the entry behavior it induces, which is why it is re-solved for each candidate belief in equations (24) and (25).

This is the identifying assumption for the entry-cost parameters: in the baseline, investors in 2014 to 2018 perceived no risk that the PTC would be withdrawn, so that the renewal probability of equation (15) equals one. The justification is institutional. In this period the credit was extended and, from the end of 2015, placed on a multi-year legislated schedule, so there was no imminent expiration date comparable to those of earlier years. The note mentions 2013 to 2018 as an alternative window.

The assumption is needed because entry costs and beliefs are not separately identified from entry rates in a single year. In equation (14) a high entry probability can come from a low threshold cost (low κ\kappaκ or a favorable ϕ\phiϕ) or from a low continuation value, and by equation (18) the continuation value is low when btb_tbt​ is low. Fixing bt=1b_t=1bt​=1 in some years removes the belief from the problem in those years: equation (18) collapses to the stationary Bellman equation (21), in which the only unknowns are (κ,ϕ)(\kappa,\phi)(κ,ϕ), and these are estimated in equation (23). The estimates are then held fixed and carried back to the earlier years, where the remaining gap between predicted and observed entry is attributed to beliefs through equation (25).

The strategy requires that the entry-cost parameters be stable over time, so that (κ,ϕ)(\kappa,\phi)(κ,ϕ) estimated on later years apply to earlier cohorts, and that the scheduled changes in subsidy levels in the stable period were foreseen and are captured by the state variables rather than by beliefs. If investors in 2014 to 2018 in fact still feared repeal, true beliefs would be below one, the estimated entry costs would be biased downward, and the earlier beliefs would be biased as well.

This is the numerical approximation used to solve the dynamic problem. The object approximated is the value function as a function of the observed state only, that is, with the private cost shock integrated out (the function Vˉ\bar VVˉ in the derivation of equation (21)); this is why νit\nu_{it}νit​ no longer appears as an argument. The ul(sit)u_l(s_{it})ul​(sit​) are known basis functions, here a quadratic basis: a constant, each state variable, and all squares and pairwise products. The γlV\gamma_l^VγlV​ are LLL unknown coefficients; with nnn continuous state variables a full quadratic basis has

L=(n+1)(n+2)2L=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}L=2(n+1)(n+2)​

terms. The note states that the profit function π(sit)\pi(s_{it})π(sit​) is approximated in the same way.

The approximation replaces an infinite-dimensional unknown function by LLL numbers. The coefficients are chosen so that the Bellman equation holds as closely as possible on a set of state points, for instance by iterating: given coefficients, compute the continuation value and the right-hand side of the integrated Bellman equation at each point, regress the result on the basis functions, and repeat until the coefficients converge. A polynomial basis combines well with the AR(1) transitions assumed for the exogenous states, because conditional expectations of the basis functions are available in closed form. If s′=a0+a1s+es'=a_0+a_1s+es′=a0​+a1​s+e with E[e]=0E[e]=0E[e]=0 and variance σe2\sigma_e^2σe2​, then

so the expected next-period value is again a quadratic function of the current state and no numerical integration over GGG is needed. The cost is approximation error: a quadratic cannot capture strong nonlinearities of the value function, and accuracy should be judged by the size of the Bellman residuals. The same device is applied to V0V^0V0 and to V1V^1V1 for each candidate belief in equation (24).

This is the estimator of the entry-cost parameters, a nonlinear least squares (minimum distance) criterion that matches entry rates in the stable-policy period in which bt=1b_t=1bt​=1, equation (20). The observed entry rate PmtEP_{mt}^EPmtE​ is the share of potential entrants in state mmm and year ttt (projects in the interconnection queue for at least two years) that enter in that year. The predicted rate averages the individual model probabilities over the NmtN_{mt}Nmt​ potential entrants of that state and year:

The estimator has a nested structure. For each trial value of (κ,ϕ)(\kappa,\phi)(κ,ϕ) the inner step solves the Bellman equation with the approximation of equation (22), which gives the continuation value and hence the predicted probabilities; the outer step searches over (κ,ϕ)(\kappa,\phi)(κ,ϕ). The profit function is not re-estimated here: π(sit)\pi(s_{it})π(sit​) comes from the bargaining, non-utility demand and buyer choice estimates of the first stage, and β\betaβ is fixed.

Identification is as follows. The scale ϕ\phiϕ is identified by the level of entry rates given profits and by how strongly entry rates respond to variation in profits across states and years, since by equation (14) the responsiveness of entry to the net gain is governed by 1/ϕ1/\phi1/ϕ. The parameter κ\kappaκ is identified by how entry rates covary with the cost shifter WitW_{it}Wit​, mainly state land prices, holding profits fixed. Matching aggregated rates rather than individual decisions makes the estimator robust to noise in the timing of individual entry, at the cost of some efficiency relative to maximum likelihood.

Three points about the notation of the note should be made explicit. First, V^1\widehat V^1V1 and V^0\widehat V^0V0 in equation (24) must be read as expected next-period values with the shock integrated out, conditional on the current state, not as the value functions evaluated at the current state. Second, the Bellman equation (17) for V0V^0V0 does not contain btb_tbt​; the argument btb_tbt​ in V^0(sit;bt)\widehat V^0(s_{it};b_t)V0(sit​;bt​) reflects the fact that the equilibrium transition of the endogenous states KmtK_{mt}Kmt​ and Φit\Phi_{it}Φit​ is re-solved for each candidate belief, which changes the expectation. Third, π^\widehat\piπ is the profit with the PTC active, π1\pi^1π1. As in equation (14), the formula applies when the term in the numerator is non-negative.

The derivative with respect to the belief, holding the value functions fixed, has the sign of −(V^1−V^0)-(\widehat V^1-\widehat V^0)−(V1−V0), and V1V^1V1 itself increases with btb_tbt​. Since the value with the subsidy exceeds the value without it, the predicted entry probability is decreasing in btb_tbt​, which is what allows the belief to be recovered from entry rates in equation (25).

This is the estimator of the policy belief of each cohort. For a given year ttt of the earlier, uncertain period it chooses the single number bt∈[0,1]b_t\in[0,1]bt​∈[0,1] that makes the model's predicted state-level entry rates as close as possible, in the least squares sense, to the observed rates PmtEP_{mt}^EPmtE​ across states mmm. The predicted rate averages the individual probabilities of equation (24) over the potential entrants of the state:

P^mtE(bt)=1Nmt∑i∈(m,t)P^tE(sit;bt).\widehat{P}_{mt}^E(b_t)=\frac{1}{N_{mt}}\sum_{i\in(m,t)}\widehat{P}_t^E(s_{it};b_t).PmtE​(bt​)=Nmt​1​i∈(m,t)∑​PtE​(sit​;bt​).

Everything else is held fixed: (κ^,ϕ^)(\hat\kappa,\hat\phi)(κ^,ϕ^​) come from the stable-policy years through equation (23), and the profit function comes from the first stage. Each evaluation of the criterion requires solving V0V^0V0 and V1V^1V1 at the candidate belief, together with the equilibrium transition of the endogenous states, so the estimator is a one-dimensional search with a fixed-point problem inside. The problem is solved separately year by year, which is possible because of the cohort-specific stationarity delivered by equation (18): the belief of year ttt affects only the decisions of year ttt.

Identification is transparent because the predicted entry rate is monotonically decreasing in btb_tbt​, as shown under equation (24). With entry costs known, there is one belief that rationalizes the overall level of entry in a year: entry above what the stable-period model predicts at bt=1b_t=1bt​=1 is attributed to a perceived risk of expiration. Cross-state variation in a single year provides over-identification, since one parameter must fit many state-level rates. The estimates in the note are about 0.30.30.3 for 2011 and about 0.840.840.84 for 2012. The interpretation rests on the maintained assumptions: any shock that raised entry in 2011 and is not captured by the profit function or the state variables is absorbed into a lower estimated belief, and beliefs are common to all investors in a year.
